context: He has just finished his spiteful prophecy of the defeat of Dante's party.

note: An obscene gesture, still known in Italy: the fist with the thumb pushed out between the first two fingers. Vanni makes it with both hands, at God.
The Italian says "friends". Dante is glad to see the snakes silence the blasphemer. Earlier in Hell he pitied sinners. By now he sides with their punishment.

context: The "ancestors" are the soldiers of Catiline, whose survivors were said to have founded the city. Dante tells Pistoia to do to itself what has just been done to Vanni: burn to ash.

quote: him who fell from Thebes' high walls
context: Until now the proudest soul Dante has met. Vanni outdoes him.

note: Half man, half horse. In Virgil's Aeneid, Cacus is a fire-breathing giant, half human, but not a centaur. Dante gives him a horse's body, and gives the fire to the dragon on his back.
The wild, swampy coast of southern Tuscany, known in Dante's time for fever and snakes.
A monstrous son of the god Vulcan who lived in a cave and preyed on the country around. Virgil tells his story in Aeneid 8, so the guide here is describing a character from his own poem.
One of the seven hills of Rome, long before the city was built.
The other centaurs, who guard the violent in the river of boiling blood (Inferno 12). Cacus was violent too, but his theft was done by a trick, so he is here among the thieves.

Hercules was driving home the cattle he had taken from the monster Geryon. Cacus stole some and dragged them backward into his cave by their tails, so that the tracks would seem to lead away from it. The lowing of the cattle gave him away.

context: In Virgil, Hercules strangles Cacus. The club comes from other Roman tellings, such as Livy's. Cacus felt barely ten of the hundred blows because he was dead by then.

note: Agnello, Buoso and Puccio, all named later in the canto. With Cianfa and Francesco, who arrive as serpents, they are five Florentine thieves from noble families. Little is known of them beyond what the early commentators say.
Cianfa Donati, of one of the great families of Florence. He has vanished because he has been turned into a snake. He is the six-legged serpent that appears a moment later.
Dante has heard a Florentine name and wants Virgil to keep quiet so he can listen.
One of the poem's direct addresses to the reader, used at moments of special wonder or weight. Dante swears to what he saw precisely because it is so hard to believe.
Cianfa Donati, in the form of a kind of lizard or dragon. He fastens on his fellow thief Agnello, and the two melt into one creature.
Thieves ignored the line between "mine" and "yours". Here they lose the line between themselves and others: even their bodies are not their own, and are stolen from them again and again.
Dante's word is papiro. It may mean paper, which was still fairly new in Italy, or a wick made of papyrus pith. Either way, the image is the brown stain that runs ahead of a flame.
Agnello Brunelleschi, of a noble Florentine family. Early commentators say he stole from childhood.
Francesco Cavalcanti, another Florentine. He is identified only in the canto's last line.

quote: where we first receive our nourishment
note: The navel, through which a child is fed in the womb.
The smoke from the snake's mouth and the man's wound mixes, and through it each takes on the other's nature. This second change is a trade, not a merging: the man becomes a snake and the snake a man.

context: In his Pharsalia, two Roman soldiers are bitten by snakes in the Libyan desert. Sabellus melts away into a pool. Nasidius swells until his armor bursts.
In the Metamorphoses, Cadmus, the founder of Thebes, is turned into a serpent, and the nymph Arethusa becomes a spring as she flees the river god Alpheus.

note: An open boast. Dante tells the two great Latin poets of transformation to be silent, because neither ever showed two creatures exchanging their natures at once. Some readers note that the pride comes in the canto of the thieves, and that Dante has borrowed freely from both.
Speech was held to be what separates humans from animals. The last thing the man loses is his tongue, and the last thing the snake gains is the power to talk.
Human spit was believed to be poisonous to snakes, so the new man's first act, along with speech, is an attack.
The man who has just become a snake. Early commentators disagree on whether he is Buoso Donati or Buoso degli Abati. Both were Florentine nobles.
Dante's word is ballast: the worthless weight in the bottom of a ship's hold. It is his name for the souls of this ditch.
An apology for any flaw in the writing, on the grounds that nothing like this had been described before.
Puccio Galigai of Florence, nicknamed Sciancato, "the Lame". He is the only one of the five who is not transformed while Dante watches.

Francesco Cavalcanti, the small snake who has just become a man again. He was killed by men of Gaville, a village in the upper Arno valley, and his family took a bloody revenge on its people. That is why Gaville weeps.
